blocks.1: My information here comes mostly from old timetables, an article in “Sogn Dagblad” of 12 December 1989 by Magnus Lundeland, and conversations with people in the village.
blocks.2: It seems that “Fylkesbaatane” had a stop here right from the start in 1858. At that time the company was called “Nordre Bergenhus Amts Dampskibe” and the stop here “Fondevig”. At the start “Fylkesbaatane” had 2 boats, iron ships, both built in Scotland. The first to arrive was “Framnes”, which was put on the Sogn route on 7 December 1858, and on 30 December came “Fjalir”, which was put on the Sunnfjord and Nordfjord route. According to the timetable “from 22 November 1859, until further notice”, “Fondevig” is a stop for both boats, both from and to Bergen.
blocks.16: And so on up the fjord.
blocks.17: On the return trip the stops are the same, but in the opposite order. The boat is then at “Fondevig” on “Saturday at 7” and in Bergen at 1.

blocks.25: And so on to Sunnfjord and Nordfjord.
blocks.26: On the trip back to Bergen the boat stopped at the same places, from “Fondevig” on “Saturday at 4”, and in Bergen at 9.
blocks.27: We see that even then Eivindvik had two boats from Bergen and two to Bergen a week. Even though it has nothing to do with Eivindvik, I would just like to mention that the comment on the timetable says, among other things: “On the way in to the Lustrafjord the steamer will, until further notice, call at AARDAL once every month”.
blocks.28: Lundeland writes that there were probably no quays in the county at the time “Fylkesbaatane” started operating, and no lighthouses along the shipping lane either. This is why the boat, on its way to Bergen from Sogn, lay in Bøfjorden from Friday evening to Saturday morning before tackling the treacherous waters along the coast to Bergen.
blocks.29: The comment on the route says that since the boat is obliged to wait for “the arrival of the Christiania post at Lærdal until 10 o'clock Friday morning”, departure times at the stops between Lærdal and Bøfjord could be up to 6 hours later than in the timetable.
blocks.30: In those days the journey from Bergen to Eivindvik took 5 hours, and it stayed that way right up until the district doctor Tom Bache-Wiig bought the doctor's boat “Eivindvik” in 1972, and through it we got a connection with “Solundir”, at Mjømna to the city and at Ånneland from the city. Both these boats were fast, and the journey time was halved, from 5 to 2 ½ hours. From 1976 Per Vold with “Thinganes” took over the feeder route that M/S “Eivindvik” had to and from the city boat. This arrangement lasted right up until we got a quay at Sollibotn in 1989 and passenger traffic went from there with the new catamarans of “Fylkesbaatane”. Then the journey time was almost halved once again.
blocks.31: As far as I can see, the stop was called “Fondevig” until 1892–93, and the agents were the owners of Fonnevik, but in 1892 Peder Rasmussen Sandal, who ran a dye works in Fonnevik, moved over to the mainland, and he also became steamer agent, probably in 1893. After this the agent's job stayed in the Sandal family until his grandson, Per Ragnar Sandal, retired as agent in May 2000.
blocks.32: At first the boats were boarded out by Tangen, I have heard; later they came into the sound. In 1901–02 Sandal built a quay.
blocks.34: Three passenger boats, one just visible on the left, at the Sandal quay in the 1930s." Photo: Unknown.
blocks.35: Eivindvik gradually became a stop with heavy traffic and many connections (transfers) between the boats. Several local routes started from Eivindvik and connected with other routes here both when they went out and when they came back. This meant that the boats spent some time lying here, and that in turn led some of the crew to settle in the place with their families. In the summer timetables for 1939 we find a total of 27 calls a week in Eivindvik. Midtunvågen was also a stop for a time when Ola Midthun kept a shop at “Stranda”.
blocks.36: Of the routes that started from Eivindvik, I mention from the timetables of 1938–40: Eivindvik – Lifjorden – Eivindvik, Eivindvik – Solund – Skifjord – Åfjord – Eivindvik, Eivindvik – Åfjord – Solund – Eivindvik, Eivindvik – Åfjorden – Eivindvik.
blocks.37: There was also a local route from Askvoll through Hyllestad and Gulen that connected here with the boat to Bergen, and one that went from here through Gulen and Solund to Askvoll.
blocks.38: One route was called Eivindvik – Høyanger – Eivindvik, and then there was the route on the Gula fjords. All these routes connected with routes to other parts of the county and to Bergen.
blocks.39: After the war (1940–45) “Fylkesbaatane” bought two English warships, which were converted into the two fine passenger boats “Sunnfjord” and “Sognefjord”. These were put in service as express boats, one on the Fjordane route and one on the Sogn route. They did not come in here, but had a regular boat stop out in the sound, and in summer they stopped almost every day, at least on the trip to Bergen. There were often several small boats out to board, and many people travelled with these express boats. The people in the small boats usually gathered in one and the same boat before boarding, so that only one boat came alongside the express boat. The boats most used for boarding were M/B “Jan”, owned by John Hellesund, and M/B “Flolid”, owned by Birger Flolid. These ferrymen became well practised and skilled at manoeuvring alongside the ship, and boarding went smoothly in “all kinds” of weather.
blocks.40: “Sognefjord” and “Sunnfjord” carried no cargo; they took the outer lane to Bergen and took 3 hours from “Eivindviksundet”, as people then called the boarding place, to Bergen.
blocks.42: Sollibotn quay: the express boat Sognekongen arrives from Bergen, and the first scheduled bus is waiting on the quay.
blocks.43: There were early plans for a quay at Stafsneset so that the express boats could come alongside and we could have a regular stop there. A decision to build was made in the 1950s, but no quay came. When “Fylkesbaatane” introduced their new express boats, the catamarans, in the 1980s, Eivindvik and district business association (founded 1986), represented by its chair Olav Midthun, among others, worked hard to get these boats to stop. At last the quay came, with a road to it, out by the shore below Sollibotn, and on Friday 14 July 1989 the catamaran “Sognekongen” came alongside for the first time, and we could travel to Bergen in under 1 ½ hours. This connection had no official opening ceremony, but people appreciated it greatly, and even though we also have bus connections with the outside world, most passenger traffic now goes via “the new quay”. Here we now have an excellent service, with boats to and from Bergen twice every weekday except Saturday, when we have one trip each way. On Sunday we have a boat to and from Bergen in the evening.
blocks.45: Cargo boat traffic still went via the Sandal quay, three boats from Bergen and two to Bergen a week. In the spring of 1994 a bus route was started to and from the quay at Sollibotn; the bus ran for the first time on 1 April.
blocks.47: (Later what remains of the cargo routes has also been moved to the quay at Sollibotn. Most goods transport now goes, here as in most places, mainly by lorry. The agents for the boat routes at Sollibotn are Leif Nyhammer and Edvard Fosse.)
